title: Assent belongs to faith’s essence — Ames departs from common Reformed doctrine
source_text: XCIV. De ipso assensu dubitant nonnulli an sit actus fidei formalis & essentialis: ut observavimus supra de Amesio, qui docet assensum esse actum fidei, non proprie ipsam fidem; quam constituit potius in quibusdam voluntatis actibus a nobis ante recensitis. Sed Amesius in eo deserit communem doctrinam Scholae Reformatae, quae statuit cum reliquis omnibus Scholis Christianis, assensum ad fidei essentiam pertinere. Et certe quis cum aliqua ratione negare possit credere Evangelio sicut oportet, esse fidei actum? At credere sicut oportet Evangelio, quid est aliud quam ei debito modo assentire? Et nonne Paulus ipse expresse ponit ut actum fidei salvificae, credere quod Deus Jesum suscitavit a mortuis?
pass_a_gloss: Concerning assent itself some doubt whether it is the formal and essential act of faith: as we observed above concerning Ames, who teaches that assent is an act of faith, not properly faith itself; which he rather constitutes in certain acts of the will previously recounted by us. But Ames in that deserts the common doctrine of the Reformed School, which with all the remaining Christian Schools lays down that assent pertains to the essence of faith. And certainly who with any reason can deny that to believe the Gospel as one ought is an act of faith? But to believe the Gospel as one ought — what else is it than to assent to it in the due manner? And does not Paul himself expressly set as an act of saving faith, to believe that God raised Jesus from the dead?
pass_b_english: Some (Ames) doubt whether assent is faith’s formal essential act — calling assent an act of faith but locating faith itself in certain will-acts.
Le Blanc: Ames leaves common Reformed (and all Christian schools’) doctrine that assent belongs to faith’s essence.
To believe the Gospel as one ought is nothing but due assent — and Paul names believing God raised Jesus as a saving-faith act.
